Different pieces, the same amount

Split each piece again and watch the numbers change while the shaded amount stays still.

A second fold changes the labels

Fold a paper strip in half and shade one half. Fold it again so the whole strip has four equal sections. The shaded area now covers two sections.

You can describe that same area as 1/2 or 2/4. These are equivalent fractions: different written fractions with the same value. Folding did not add or remove any shaded paper.

Try it yourself

Choose a multiplier for the number of pieces. The top strip stays as one half. The bottom strip cuts both the selected half and the unselected half into more equal parts.

With a multiplier of three, each original half becomes three smaller pieces. There are six pieces in the whole and three selected pieces: 1/2 = 3/6. Both strips cover exactly the same length.

+

Try it yourself

More pieces, same half

Cut each half again. Watch the shaded length stay the same.

Change both numbers in the same way

To create an equivalent fraction, multiply the numerator and denominator by the same positive whole number. Starting from 2/3, multiplying both by two gives 4/6. Each third has been split into two sixths.

Adding the same number to the top and bottom does not follow this rule. For example, 1/2 and 2/3 are different amounts. A quick sketch makes that difference visible.

You can go back to larger pieces

Four eighths can be regrouped as two quarters, then one half. We call writing the fraction with smaller whole-number terms simplifying. Its value stays the same.

A useful check is to ask whether both numbers were divided by the same number with whole-number results. For 6/8, dividing both by two gives 3/4. Dividing only the numerator would change the amount.
